body:
We make Kiron, and our founding team ran a push/pull/legs split in Strong for many years. Everything here about Strong and Hevy comes from their App Store listings, their help pages and recent App Store reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

Strong is a workout log: you write your routines (a saved workout for each training day), and it records every set, quickly. It has been on the App Store since 2011, and people who leave are rarely unhappy with the logging. Of its 500 most recent US App Store reviews, 186 give 1 to 3 stars; 68 of those mention the Apple Watch app and 33 mention price or the paywall (we counted by keyword, so treat these as rough). A few ask for a plan or automatic weight increases.

Here's how Kiron (that's us) compares, when Hevy fits better, and when to stay with Strong.

Strong or Kiron? The short answer

  • Choose Kiron if you like Strong's habit of opening the app and doing the next workout, but want the plan written and every weight worked out for you. Start from one of {{kiron:program-count}} ready-made programs or your own.
  • Stay with Strong if you log on an Apple Watch, already own Strong's lifetime plan, or just want a plain log of routines you write, which Strong does for less money.
  • Want a different log, not a plan? Hevy is the closest thing to Strong, with a social feed and apps for Apple Watch and Android watches.
  • Switching is easy: Kiron imports your Strong history and starts your weights from it.

Bottom line: both apps keep the gym simple. Strong leaves the plan and the weights to you; Kiron handles both. If you'd rather not write routines or work out when to add weight, that's what Kiron is for.

What Kiron is

Kiron is a workout app for {{kiron:cell-platforms}} that runs your training plan for you. Start in one of three ways:

  • Pick a ready-made program. There are {{kiron:program-count}}, sorted by goal, from Beginner 5×5 and Push / Pull / Legs to a first 5K or a marathon. Many follow formats lifters and runners have used for decades.
  • Answer a few questions and Kiron builds one.
  • Bring your own plan. Paste it from ChatGPT, a coach or a website, or snap a photo, and Kiron turns it into a program.

From then on:

  • Your next workout is waiting when you open the app, whether you train on set days or whenever you get to the gym.
  • Every weight is worked out for you, from the first session, and raised as you get stronger (more below).
  • Variety that keeps your main lifts. Smaller exercises can change week to week; the big lifts stay, so you can watch them climb.
  • Travel and short days are covered. Save a hotel or second gym with its equipment, or shorten today's workout in a few taps.
  • Runs and race plans share the calendar with your lifting.
  • Recovery counts your other workouts, like runs and rides that other apps save to Apple Health or Health Connect.
  • {{kiron:progress-lead}} {{kiron:progress-detail}} {{kiron:progress-import}}
  • {{kiron:offline-lead}} {{kiron:offline-detail}}

{{kiron:pricing-sentence}}

Strong's simple routine, with the homework done

Strong's appeal is speed: write your routines once, then at the gym open the next one and log each set. In the same 500 reviews, 103 of the 314 with four or five stars call it simple, fast, easy or intuitive.

Our founding team trained this way for many years, running a push/pull/legs split in Strong and simply doing the next day of the program each time we got to the gym.

Kiron's Whenever I train setting works exactly like that: your program stays in order, the next workout waits on the Today screen marked "Up next", and a day off never counts as missed. Lifting programs, like Kiron's Push / Pull / Legs, start this way. Prefer set days? Switch to Fixed days, and Kiron can move a missed workout for you.

The difference is the homework. In Strong, the plan and every weight are yours to work out. In Kiron:

  • Every lift starts at a sensible weight, worked out from your history (a little lighter after time off), a related lift or a safe standard, with the reason on the exercise: "You did 100 lb × 8 on EZ Bar Curl, so we started Hammer Curl at 35 lb per hand." Then Kiron asks "How did 35 lb feel?" (Too easy, Just right or Too hard) and adjusts the sets you have left.
  • Weights go up when you've earned it, with the reason on screen: "You hit every set, so we added 5 lb."

Strong's App Store page also lists $3.99, $23.99 and $79.99 versions and 6 months for $19.99; above are the prices its description gives. Prices vary by country and offer.

Paying monthly, Kiron is {{kiron:price-monthly}}, or {{kiron:price-monthly-yearly}} if you keep it all year, so if you're staying, its yearly plan saves about 58%.

If you only want a different log: Hevy

Hevy works like Strong (you write routines and log your sets) and adds a social feed for following friends, apps for Apple Watch and Android watches, and a web version. Pro, at $23.99 a year or $74.99 once, includes Hevy Trainer, which builds a lifting program from your goals, equipment and schedule and tells you when to add weight.

Like Kiron, Hevy imports Strong's file: your finished workouts come across, though routines don't. One caution if the Watch is why you're leaving: 4 of Hevy's 15 low-star reviews from late October to mid-November 2026 mention the Watch too. More in Hevy vs Kiron.

Moving from Strong, history and all

  1. Export from Strong. In Strong's Settings, tap Export Strong Data (Export Data on Android). You get a CSV file, a plain table of every set you've logged.
  2. Start Kiron. Pick a program or paste your plan.
  3. Bring your history. In Kiron's Settings, tap Import from another app and choose Strong's file. Strong's file often doesn't say whether it's in pounds or kilograms, so Kiron shows your heaviest set and asks. Then it shows how it matched each exercise before saving, and you can remove the import later.
  4. Train. Lifts in your Strong history start from your last numbers, a little lighter if it's been a while. Anything new gets a suggested weight and a note saying why.
  5. Cancel Strong Pro where you subscribed, if you pay for it.

Strong can't import that file back, and Kiron has no export of its own, so keep it safe. Our guide to exporting your workout history covers five other apps too, and what to do with the file in a spreadsheet.

Who should stay with Strong

  • You want a log and nothing more. If you know your plan by heart and like choosing your own weights, Strong does that one job quickly, and has since 2011.
  • You log on your wrist. Strong has an Apple Watch app, and 34 of those 314 four- and five-star reviews mention the Watch, mostly warmly. Kiron has no Watch app; it reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect afterwards.
  • Price comes first. Strong Pro is $29.99 a year, or $99.99 once for good, and its free version logs unlimited workouts with up to 3 routines. Kiron is {{kiron:price-annual}}, with no lifetime plan or free version. If you already own Strong's lifetime plan, any other app is new money.
  • You value a long track record. Strong has more than 108,000 ratings on the US App Store, averaging 4.9. Kiron is new and still small.

Questions about leaving Strong

Is Strong free, or is there a free alternative?

Strong's free version logs unlimited workouts but keeps only 3 routines, so a push/pull/legs split fits and a plan with four different days doesn't. Pro removes the limit. Hevy's free plan holds 4 routines and 7 custom exercises, per its help center, and Boostcamp's free tier includes most of its coach-made programs. A spreadsheet costs nothing too. {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}

Is Strong Pro worth it?

If you like Strong and need more than 3 routines, probably. Lifetime, at $99.99, equals about three years and four months of yearly Pro. Pro doesn't write a plan or choose your weights, though; that's the job Kiron does.

Can I move my Strong history to another app?

Yes. Kiron and Hevy both import Strong's file (Kiron takes Fitbod and Hevy files too), and the Kiron steps are above. Routines don't move to either app, because Strong's file holds finished workouts only.

Why isn't Strong syncing with my Apple Watch?

It's the most common complaint in Strong's low-star reviews. Strong's October 2026 update (6.5.1) fixed sign-ins that could lapse and quietly stop syncing, so update and sign in again if asked. Several reviewers also lost sets logging on the phone and the Watch in one workout, so use one device at a time. If it still fails, contact Strong's support.

If you like Strong's simple routine but want the plan written and the weights worked out for you, try Kiron. Pick Push / Pull / Legs or any of the {{kiron:program-count}} programs, or paste your own, bring your Strong history, and do the next workout whenever you get to the gym. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If a log is all you need and Strong suits you, staying put is a good answer.
